info.bio:
Coldplay es una banda británica de estilo Britpop/Rock alternativo. Se formó en 1998, y es conocida por sus letras suaves e introspectivas.

Los miembros de Coldplay se conocieron en la Universidad de Londres en septiembre de 1996. Primero se juntaron Martin y Buckland, y ya para el 8 de enero de 1998, Coldplay completó su formación, al unirse Will Champion. Él sabía tocar el piano, la guitarra y el bajo, y aunque no sabía tocar la batería, aprendió rápidamente.

scenes.name: Brit-pop y post-pop
scenes.author: Piero Scaruffi
scenes.desc: Como tantas veces, el fenómeno más publicitado es el menos interesante: un «brit-pop» de grupos terriblemente parecidos y tediosos, sin apenas imaginación. Lo anticipan Lightning Seeds, La's, Teenage Fanclub y Heavenly; estalla con Boo Radleys, Blur (Parklife) y Oasis (el «farol» que mejor personifica la moda). Suede y el glam-pop (Super Furry Animals, Placebo), las excepciones de High Llamas (Hawaii) y Supergrass, el revival mod (Ocean Colour Scene, Wildhearts), Elastica, Sleeper, las Spice Girls; Trembling Blue Stars, Tindersticks, Delgados. El post-pop de Radiohead, «la banda más publicitada y sobrevalorada de la década», cuyo OK Computer es una obra maestra del falso vanguardismo; Coldplay, Travis.

mentions.author: Piero Scaruffi
mentions.text: …generation of 1997-98: Six By Seven, whose The Things We Make (1998) was basically a neurotic version of the "Madchester" sound of the Stone Roses; Coldplay, whose Parachuttes (2000) was mainly a display of dynamic and emotional ranges; Travis; Dream City Film Club; etc. Teen-pop The real million-sellers…

podcast.title: Eighth Highest Earner (2016)
podcast.body: Coldplay earned 88 million dollars in 2016, placing them eighth on the Forbes list. Their success is notable for generating high income from relatively few, but extremely profitable, concerts. The band structured their tour to average 5 million dollars per concert, which was, by far, the highest income per performance for any artist that year. "ha montado una gira de tal manera que han llegado a ingresar una media de 5 millones de dólares por concierto."

podcast.title: 21st Century Rock Success
podcast.body: Coldplay was mentioned as one of the few bands from the first decade of the 21st century that could potentially "rank against the alt rock giants of the 80s and 90s," highlighting a perceived lack of new rock superstars. "Now think about it, outside of Coldplay, Jack White, Gorillas and maybe Lincoln Park. Who else from the first decade of the 21st century can rank against the alt rock giants of the 80s and 90s?"

podcast.title: Ambition to Be First Band to Perform on the Moon
podcast.body: Coldplay has publicly declared their aspiration to be the first musical group to perform on the moon. This ambitious goal highlights the band's interest in pushing the boundaries of live performance. "Coldplay has announced that they want to be the first band to perform on the moon."

podcast.title: Ancestor Invented Daylight Savings Time
podcast.body: Chris Martin's great-great-grandfather is credited with originating the concept of daylight savings time, an idea that emerged prior to World War I. "The great, great grandfather of Cold Placing or Chris Martin is the guy who came up with the concept of daylight savings time in the days before World War I."

podcast.body: Coldplay is among the artists noted for using backward messages, particularly in the era of digital sound editing software, which became widely available in the late 1990s and early 2000s. "Back, cake, cold play, M&M, Fransford Nand, Lincoln Park, Marilyn Manson, Moby Soundgarden Tool, 21 Pilots, and a ton more."

podcast.title: Backstage Rider – Extensive Towel Requirement
podcast.body: Coldplay's rider demands a substantial quantity of towels: at least 60 bath-sized towels, which translates to 15 towels per band member, highlighting a significant need for hygiene or other backstage uses. "At least 60 bath-sized towels, so 15 towels, remember? At least no American beer ever."

podcast.title: Backstage Rider – No American Beer & Past Sock Request
podcast.body: The band explicitly stipulates "no American beer ever" in their rider. Historically, Coldplay also used to request socks, a common demand for bands starting out on tour. "At least no American beer ever."

podcast.title: Car Racing and Collection
podcast.body: Guy Berryman, Coldplay's bassist, occasionally races cars under an assumed name. His collection of road cars, comprising about 25 vehicles, features a mix of vintage and new models. This includes a Bugatti Veyron (retailing for over $3 million), a Lamborghini Aventador (worth approximately $1 million), a Ferrari F40, a McLaren F1 (valued around $25 million), and several Porsches. "He has a Bugatti Veyron, which retails for well beyond $3 million. A Lamborghini Aventador, good for about a million, a Ferrari F40, a McLaren F1, which, about $25 million for one of those, and a couple of porches, about 25 cars in total."

"Ed Sheeran, Coldplay, Led Zeppelin, Katy Perry, Lady Gaga, and dozens more have all been wrapped up in these controversies."

podcast.title: Echoing Kraftwerk
podcast.body: Coldplay deliberately echoed Kraftwerk's style in a 2005 song, which became a major hit single globally. This direct influence led to Kraftwerk receiving songwriting credits for the track, contributing to the "X&Y" album's sales of over 15 million copies. "Here's Coldplay, deliberately echoing Craftwork in 2005. And before you ask, yes, Craftwork does get songwriting credits on this Coldplay song."

podcast.body: Coldplay's tours are identified as having surpassed the box office achievements of U2's 360 tour, demonstrating their significant financial success and draw in the global concert scene. "Ed Sheeran, Elton John, Coldplay, and Taylor Swift have eclipsed that."

podcast.body: Will Champion of Coldplay is among the contemporary drummers who have embraced modern electronic drums. These kits are used to trigger a variety of sounds, tones, patterns, and samples to suit their musical needs. "Today's electronic drums have been embraced by players such as Danny Carey, Neil Peart, Will Champion of Coldplay, Rob Borden of Lincoln Park, and many, many others."

podcast.title: Extensive Car Collection from Music Success
podcast.body: As the bass player for Coldplay, Guy Berryman has amassed a significant car collection, reported to be around 25 vehicles. His infatuation with cars began in childhood. His collection includes a unique 1957 Porsche 356-Carrera Speedster built for a French racing driver, a Bugatti Veyron (once the fastest production car at nearly 430 km/h), Ferraris, Lamborghinis, Lancias, and Alpines. He occasionally races these cars on the track, which is financially feasible due to Coldplay's success with tens of millions of albums sold, billions of streams, and equally divided royalties. "As the bass player for Coldplay, the music business has been very, very good to Guy Barryman."

podcast.title: Goofy Song for Chris Martin's Child
podcast.body: Coldplay formed the pseudonymous band The Nappys to record a goofy song and accompanying video called "I'm Your Baby's Daddy." This project was a personal endeavor by Chris Martin, dedicated to his then-wife Gwyneth Paltrow while she was expecting their first child, affectionately referred to as "Little Apple." Sir George Martin notably introduced the video in a curly red wig. "When she was expecting Little Apple, the band got together for a goofy song and video under the name The Nappy's."

podcast.title: Influence of David Bowie
podcast.body: Coldplay's sound and vision contain "bits of Bowie DNA," indicating a clear influence from David Bowie's work. "Nirvana, the sex pistols, the food fighters, nine inch nails, REM smashing pumpkins, the killers, Scott Wyland, Coldplay. They all have bits of Bowie DNA in their sound and vision."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Leading Eco-Friendly Music Practices
podcast.body: Coldplay is recognized as a major act that has done more than most to adopt eco-friendly practices in the music industry. Their concerts are powered by renewable energy, including solar panels, fan-powered bikes that generate electricity, and kinetic floors that harness crowd movement. They collaborate with BMW to develop rechargeable battery systems, plant a tree for every ticket sold, donate to environmental causes, and prioritize electric trains or buses for travel between gigs. Their merchandise uses minimal plastic, single-use plastics are phased out at shows, and their staging is designed for energy efficiency. "They have probably done more in this area than any other major act. Concerts are powered through renewable energy, not just solar panels, but they have bikes that fans can ride to generate power."

podcast.title: Live Performance Success
podcast.body: By 2008, Coldplay was considered one of the "big boys" in the alt-rock universe, along with bands like Foo Fighters, Weezer, Pearl Jam, and U2. They demonstrated their ability to draw massive audiences, selling millions of concert tickets despite comparatively lower record sales in the post-Napster era. "While the big boys, like the Foo Fighters and Coldplay and Weezer and Pearl Jam and you too, continued to do their thing for the latter half of the Zero-Zero's, a couple of trends and movements emerged in the Alt Rock universe."

Their success is largely driven by Chris Martin's use of the piano as his primary instrument, which features prominently in many of their hit songs. "The most commercially successful piano based band to come out of the Al Rock world is arguably cold play."

podcast.title: Settlement with Joe Satriani
podcast.body: Coldplay faced a lawsuit from Joe Satriani over similarities between "Viva La Vida" and his song "If I Could Fly." Although Coldplay "denied any wrongdoing and did not admit any kind of guilt," a "settlement that was sealed by the court" was reached, and Satriani "went away with a settlement and has kept his word by keeping all the details secret." "Action was taken, a settlement was reached, and everybody moved on."

xref.title: Immense Influence on New Rock
xref.body: David Bowie is considered uniquely influential in the world of New Rock, with his work in the 1970s being traceable as a root for genres like punk, new wave, industrial, and electronic music. His influence is evident in the sound and vision of numerous bands including Nirvana, the Sex Pistols, Foo Fighters, Nine Inch Nails, R.E.M., Smashing Pumpkins, The Killers, Scott Weiland, and Coldplay. He is described as "the Beatles of the alt rock set." "Take any genre of rock you like punk, new wave, industrial electronic and somehow you'll be able to trace it back to something that David Bowie did in the 1970s."
